text: Late in the Vietnam War, the coffins reaching Latino neighborhoods arrived often enough that a young man could keep the count himself. Efrain Gutierrez shot eighty-one minutes in Spanish, close to the ground, and the argument his protagonist works through is not with the war as policy but with its arithmetic: who gets asked, who gets spared, and what a place in society is worth at that price. The anger stays domestic in scale. It is measured in brothers and blocks, not in nations. Later the National Film Registry took the film in; in 1976 it was a Spanish-language feature addressed to the audience it was about, and the question it puts about belonging comes from someone still young enough to expect an answer.

In 1917 fifty minutes was enough for one situation, and the situation here is two sisters pulling in opposite directions. One plays music and has attached herself to a man who will cost her something; the other runs wild and is watched from a distance by a carpenter too shy to speak. John H. Collins arranges the four of them so that every attachment is legible to everyone except the person inside it. What carries now is where the era puts its moral weight: words like soul, ruin and worth land on the sisters, while the men who set the trouble in motion are simply men with intentions. Melodrama at this length works by contrast — keyboard against workbench, parlour against open air — and by the cruelty of timing, since in a place this size the wrong suitor is always already in the room.

The mill grinds the tenants' grain and it is also where the landowner waits, and the couple who farm his fields are in no position to name the difference. Lee Man-hee set this in years when the policeman in a Korean village answered to Japan, and that one fact fixes the limits of what anyone here can do about anything. The husband works land he will never hold. His wife has become a term the old man has added to the rent. Ninety-two minutes lets the pressure build the way debt builds, by increments nobody chooses, and the film attends less to the landowner's appetite than to what the arrangement does to the hours the couple still spend in their own house. The story could be told as scandal. It is told instead as an account of the route by which a household's poverty becomes one woman's obligation.

August 29, 1970: a march in East Los Angeles, a student crew from UCLA, and a film that changed its subject while it was being shot. The plan was to document the Chicano Moratorium against the war in Vietnam. What David García and his collaborators came away with was the police response, the chaos that followed, and then the inquest into the death of Ruben Salazar, a journalist the movement had already made a figure of. Thirty-one minutes, cut so the street runs up against the hearing room, where the proceedings keep a composure the footage will not support. It was the first collective project of UCLA's Ethno-Communications Program, and it survives in a strange condition: the original elements vanished more than forty years ago, so what plays now is a copy of a copy — a film about an official account failing, itself preserved only as loss of detail.

No older Korean film has survived, which puts a great deal of weight on seventy-three minutes about a servant with nothing to show for his labour. Young-bok spent seven years in his fiancé's household as a man-servant and was put out of the door. He turns up next at Gyoung-sung station, working among arrivals and departures that are not his. Ahn Jong-hwa keeps the film at the level of wages, lodging and debts owed, so the melodrama accumulates out of ordinary accounting rather than fate; the KOFA hundred carries it, though what holds attention is the specificity of a story about being owed. A railway station is the right setting for a man with nowhere to be. Everyone there is on the way somewhere, and he is at work.

The camera is inside the California Institution for Women, and most of the talking is done by the people the film was made with rather than about. Kathy Levitt worked with the Women's Film Workshop and a group of inmates; forty-eight minutes, nearly all of it videotape transferred to film. The electronic image carries its own claim — this was the equipment available, and it was sufficient. Statistics turn up here and there, and they are the weakest material in it, because the speakers handle the analysis themselves: race, sex, religion, class, money, drugs, and what any of them has to do with who ends up inside. Only the opening and closing footage was shot beyond the walls, which sets every conversation between two glimpses of a world the speakers are not currently in. The National Film Registry took it in, and the anger in it has not aged into history.

A diary that admits to being staged is an odd object: the intimacy is real, the occasion for it is manufactured. Stanton Kaye and the woman he was involved with play themselves through eighty-seven minutes of vignettes, which means every scene has two authors who are also its subject. By 1969 the equipment was light enough for a couple to point it at their own kitchen, and the temptation of that was to call whatever came out of it the truth. Kaye declines. He builds the record and leaves the seams where they can be seen. What accumulates is less a portrait of a relationship than an account of how fast two people learn to perform for a machine they own, and of the point at which the performance starts standing in for the thing it was meant to preserve.

Greene County, Alabama, filmed in 1976 by someone who grew up there and came back with a camera. Mort Jordan was a student at Temple at the time, and the fifty-one minutes he assembled are made of vignettes and people talking in their own words. Two kinds of memory sit side by side: a fondness among some residents for values they place in the past, and the patience of people who were told their turn was coming and have stopped treating the request as reasonable. Jordan stages no confrontation between them. He lets the two accounts of one county run in parallel, which is harder to set aside than an argument would be. The film arrives once the movement had become something spoken of in the past tense, and its elegy is for the interval — the years of waiting, and what the waiting cost the people doing it.

Sixteen minutes is not long enough to argue a case; it is long enough to look at one thing steadily. Robert A. Nakamura's short takes Manzanar as its subject, the camp where Japanese Americans were held during the war, and he made it in 1971, when the people who had been confined there were still in the middle of their working lives. A documentary this brief cannot assemble authorities or balance testimony against testimony; it has to pick a vantage and stay there, and the picking is the film. The Academy Film Archive preserved it in 2011. The proportion is what stays: years taken out of many lives, addressed in the space of a single reel, with no attempt made to close that gap by adding running time.

The watchtower went up on a Yongsan rooftop and stood for twenty-five hours. Tenants facing eviction built it because appealing by ordinary means had got them nowhere, and when the police unit went in, six people died — five evictees and one officer. Afterwards the survivors were the ones charged. Kim Il-ran's documentary works inside the record that followed: the prosecutors' finding that the fault lay with an illegal and violent demonstration, set against the contrary reading in which the crackdown itself turned a clearance into a catastrophe. A hundred and one minutes of competing accounts, held apart rather than reconciled. What it makes visible is how much of what a country settles about a death is settled in the words chosen to describe it.

Everything in it was shot by someone else; the authorship lies entirely in the order of the cuts. Fox Movietone News assembled the picture out of stock and archive material, including footage from national collections that had been closed, and hung it on Lawrence Stallings's book, running from the war's beginning to its end. The method is juxtaposition. Trench footage against European royalty photographed at home; actions at sea against interiors where nothing is at risk. No commentary needs to press the point, because the cut has made it already. Seventy-eight minutes of compilation asks a different kind of work than staging does — the decisions are all adjacency and length — and the National Board of Review put the result among its ten films of the year. A film of this sort cannot invent anything. It can only decide what follows what.

A coach running a girls' basketball team is using heroin, and the boy his household has just taken in is twelve years old. Jessie Maple directed this in 1981, seventy-three minutes now on the National Film Registry, and the obligations lie on top of one another without resolving: practices to run, a kid off the street to raise, a habit to keep out of sight of both. Addiction is neither spectacle nor lesson here. It is a scheduling problem, which is nearer to how it works — the day gets built around it, and somebody is always left waiting somewhere. The gym supplies a place with rules; at home the rules are improvised hour by hour. What a production this size gains in exchange for what it lacks is proximity: rooms at their actual dimensions, players who move like players, mentorship carried out in the time left over.

Nearly eight hours of unshaped material: no cut for release, no commentary, no order imposed after the fact. George Stevens shot it for the US Army Signal Corps between 1944 and 1946, and the assignment ran from the Normandy landings through the liberation of Paris to Dachau. Raw footage declines the service a finished documentary performs, which is to say where to look and for how long. Rolls end mid-gesture. The camera stays on things an edit would remove, and the labour becomes visible: a man deciding, in the moment, what will be worth having later. It is listed on the National Film Registry as footage rather than as a picture, and the distinction is worth keeping. The deciding — where to stand at Dachau, when to start the camera — is itself the document.

Cab Calloway kept a camera running at home between 1948 and 1951, and fifty-six minutes of what he shot survives. His wife Nuffie appears in more of it than anyone. The rest is their house on Long Beach, and roads, hotels and shorelines from trips that carried them across North and South America. None of it was made to explain a career. Home movies by a performer are a peculiar kind of record, since a man who has spent his working life composing an image for audiences is here on the other side of the lens, settling what a private life looks like while it is being filmed by one of the two people inside it. Footage like this sits between arrangement and accident, and the interest of it is duration: a marriage photographed at the length it actually takes, by someone with no reason to cut anything short.
